classification.difficultyReason: Coordinate intercepts, curve order and asymptotic behaviour on common axes, then use the inverse relationship to sketch the logarithmic curve on the same axes as its exponential.

content.prompt: On the same set of axes, sketch the following sets of curves.

answer.short: All three curves increase through $(0,1)$ and approach $y=0$ on the left.
answer.worked: All three curves pass through $(0,1)$. At $x=1$ their heights are $2$, $3$ and $4$, respectively. For $x>0$, $4^x>3^x>2^x$. The order reverses for $x<0$. Draw the three curves increasing and approaching $y=0$ on the left.

spec.description: Three increasing exponentials on common axes with one y-axis tick and matched standard blue, red and green curve labels.
spec.mathematics: y=2^x, y=3^x and y=4^x intersect at (0,1) and approach y=0 to the left.

answer.short: All three curves decrease through $(0,1)$ and approach $y=0$ on the right.
answer.worked: Replacing $x$ with $-x$ reflects each curve in part (a) across the $y$-axis. All three still pass through $(0,1)$. At $x=-1$ their heights are $2$, $3$ and $4$, respectively. Draw the three curves decreasing and approaching $y=0$ on the right.

spec.description: Three decreasing exponentials on common axes with one y-axis tick. The standard blue, red and green curve labels match the same bases as in part (a).
spec.mathematics: y=2^{-x}, y=3^{-x} and y=4^{-x} intersect at (0,1) and approach y=0 to the right.

answer.short: The two curves are reflections in $y=x$.
answer.worked: Sketch $y=2^x$ through $(0,1)$ and $(1,2)$, approaching $y=0$ on the left. Reflect it in $y=x$ to sketch $y=\log_2 x$ through $(1,0)$ and $(2,1)$. The reflected curve approaches $x=0$ from the right as $y$ decreases.

spec.sourceRegion: Exercise 8A Q5(c), lower left above Q6
spec.description: Exponential and logarithmic curves with a dashed reflection line, directly labelled in standard blue. Equal units on both axes preserve the reflection geometry.
spec.mathematics: y=2^x and y=log_2(x) are inverse functions. Their intercepts (0,1) and (1,0) reflect across y=x.
